text: A poacher's living depends on knowing which parts of the woods nobody is watching. The man at the center of Furtivos has that knowledge and not much else; the house he sleeps in belongs to his mother, and so, in every arrangement that matters, does he. Then a girl who has run from a reform school comes through it, and a household built for two has to decide what to do with a third. José Luis Borau allows himself eighty-two minutes, too few for any softening: tenderness and threat come out of the same gestures, and rural Spain is a set of working arrangements rather than a view. The film went out as Spain's submission to the Academy Awards, carries a Golden Shell, and turns up on Caimán's hundred-title account of Spanish cinema.

On a Hollywood lot, in a line of extras waiting to be told where to stand, is a former Imperial Russian general and cousin to the Czar. The man directing the picture came up out of the revolution that ended him. Josef von Sternberg gets eighty-eight minutes from that arrangement, and the interest is not in who won; it is in what a studio does with a real past. It hires it by the day, costumes it, and points a camera at it. Rank travels here, but only as wardrobe. The Academy named the film for Best Actor and for Best Story, and it later entered the National Film Registry and TIME's All-TIME 100 - durable company for a picture about the rate at which a life becomes material for somebody else's production.

The subject here is a job of work: one man trying to get a tree onto canvas before the light and the season move past him. Víctor Erice filmed the painter Antonio Lopez at that task and let the pace of the painting set the pace of the film, so that measurement, waiting and weather become the events. It carries a Jury Prize and sits on TSPDT's thousand and on Caimán's hundred of Spanish cinema, unusual company for a hundred and thirty-eight minutes of somebody working. The length is the argument, though: the difficulty cannot be summarized without being falsified. The stake is small and complete. A painting made from life competes with its own subject, and only one of the two is under any obligation to hold still.

Rita cuts hair for a living and signs up for a literature course, which turns out to be a negotiation over how she is allowed to speak. Her tutor has a marriage in pieces, a bottle he needs to get through the day, and a subject he has stopped believing in. The Academy marked the film in three categories and the BFI later placed it among a hundred British films, a lot of attention for a hundred and six minutes of two people arguing in one room. Lewis Gilbert keeps the camera near them and lets the class system stay audible in every sentence: she wants the vocabulary that gets a person taken seriously, and he has begun to suspect that his own is a hiding place. Each is right about the other, which is what the arrangement costs.

Charity is the least controversial thing a wealthy woman can do, and Roberto Rossellini stages it as an emergency. A Roman socialite loses her young son; guilt pushes her into the parts of the city her class has arranged not to see, and she gives her time, then her money, then more than the arrangement can absorb. Her husband objects early. The lead performance holds a Volpi Cup, and the film appears on Italy's hundred-to-save register and on TSPDT's thousand, but the pressure in its hundred and eighteen minutes comes from the second half of the premise: the question of her sanity, raised by people who are all behaving reasonably by their own lights. Goodness, pursued past the point of decoration, reads from outside as symptom.

The drive south begins as comedy: a Milan factory supervisor bringing his northern wife home to the Sicily where everyone knew him before he was anybody. Alberto Lattuada lets that hold for a long stretch - the film is funny, and an old oath waits at the edge of the frame while it is being funny. It holds a Golden Shell and sits among the Italian films the country has marked to keep. What the man stands to lose is not his life but the fiction his life rests on, which is that leaving was a completed act. A hundred and five minutes, and the register changes without the tone changing at all; that is the difficulty the picture sets itself, and the reason the obligation, when it is called in, arrives with the weight of an errand.

A girl is born into a line of succession her grandfather insists cannot include her. The refusal is the machine of the film, and Niki Caro is careful to make it cost him: he is not a villain but a leader with an inheritance to place and a conviction about who can hold it, and the conviction is failing in front of him. The Māori community here is not backdrop; the duty being argued over is specific, and the argument has terms the film takes the trouble to lay out. A hundred and one minutes, told at a child's eye level and never once stooping to it. The lead performance drew Academy notice for Best Actress, and the film later joined the BBC's hundred greatest films directed by women, where it stands as a domestic story about who is permitted to inherit.

This time the joke has a second person in it, and she takes it over: Borat travels with his daughter, and the film keeps handing her the harder material. Fourteen years after the first trip, the return is made into a country mid-pandemic and mid-election, which sets a production problem nobody had to invent - the material would not hold still and could not be scheduled. Ninety-six minutes. The Academy marked the supporting performance and the screenplay, filed under adapted, a strange classification for a sequel and an exact one for a picture borrowing a character the audience has already consented to. It took the Golden Globe for musical or comedy. The method has not changed; what is new is that somebody in the frame has something to lose.

A student council race decides nothing, which is why the adults involved in it have no cover at all. Alexander Payne puts a high school teacher opposite a student whose ambition is not a phase and will not be embarrassed out of her, and the comedy works the gap between what the teacher believes he is doing and what he is doing. A hundred and three minutes, an American high school photographed without nostalgia, and a moral argument conducted almost entirely through small administrative decisions. It carries the Writers Guild award for adapted screenplay and an Independent Spirit for best feature, with Academy notice for the script as well. What it finally examines is how much of a grown man's self-regard depends on a teenager not getting what she wants.

Seven hundred and fifty million dollars, payable on a single condition: that Arthur marry the woman his family has picked out. He is thirty, and the film's own word for him is child - a man never once required to want something that could not be arranged. That is the comic engine and also the diagnosis. Steve Gordon builds the picture out of exchanges rather than incidents, so the pressure sits in the dialogue, where an inheritance can be discussed as a wage and a marriage as the work that earns it. Ninety-seven minutes. The Academy marked a lead performance, a supporting one and the original screenplay, the Writers Guild recognized the writing too, and the Golden Globe for musical or comedy went the same way.

An angel moves too early and takes a quarterback out of a body that still had seasons left in it. The correction is administrative: the man is owed the rest of his life, the record says so, and a replacement body has to be located before anything else can proceed. Buck Henry plays this flat, at the tempo of a clerical apology, which is what keeps a hundred and one minutes of fantasy from curdling into whimsy. The Academy marked the film for direction, for a lead performance and - rarely for a comedy - for cinematography, a sign of how much care went into surfaces that a farce could have left rough. Under the mix-up sits a plain question about continuity: what carries over, when the thing carrying it belongs to somebody else.

Twenty years of silence, and each of them still knows the other's timing better than anyone else alive. They were an act once, famous in vaudeville and unable to stand each other offstage; now a television producer, nephew to one of them, wants the reunion for a variety show. Herbert Ross runs it a hundred and eleven minutes, mostly indoors, and the Academy's notice for production design belongs to that decision - the comedy happens in rooms two men have furnished around their own retirements. The lead and supporting performances were marked as well. What holds it together is craft as physical fact: a routine two bodies can still execute exactly, and two men who cannot stay in a room long enough to execute it.

Two men in an office work out that a failure can pay better than a hit, provided nobody comes back to ask for the money. One is a Broadway producer with a technique for parting wealthy elderly investors from their checkbooks; the other is his accountant, who finds the loophole and is frightened by his own arithmetic. It sits in the National Film Registry, on TSPDT's thousand and on the Writers Guild's hundred and one screenplays, and Mel Brooks needs only eighty-nine minutes of it. The escalation is structural - each step the reasonable consequence of the one before, which is how the picture arrives at a musical in praise of Hitler and makes the arrival feel like bookkeeping. Taste is not the transgression here. The ledger is.

A man tells his wife he wants a divorce, and the evening does not stop; it continues, separately, for another two hours. John Cassavetes gives a hundred and thirty minutes to talk that has nowhere to arrive, two people out among other people, performing an ease neither of them has. Scenes are allowed to run past the point at which they have made their point. It carries a Volpi Cup for best actor, a place in the National Film Registry, and Academy notice in both supporting categories and for the original screenplay. The marriage is not the suspense. It is the given, withdrawn in the first minutes, and what the film watches is how a night gets filled once the thing that had been organizing it is taken away.
